system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-12-16 03:04:00 to 2155-12-21 18:51:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for two weeks of intermittent diarrhea, abdominal distension, and chills, with acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration. Workup revealed no infectious cause, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) was diagnosed as the likely etiology. She was treated with rifaximin and hyoscyamine, along with dietary modifications, leading to resolution of diarrhea and improvement in symptoms. Renal function normalized with IV fluids. Imaging showed a new L1 compression fracture and a slightly enlarged pancreatic cyst, both of which were managed conservatively with follow-up plans. She remained stable, completed treatment, and was discharged home with outpatient GI follow-up for pancreatic lesion monitoring.
problems: Pathologic fracture of other specified site
Secondary diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, not stated as uncontrolled, or unspecified
Bacterial infection, unspecified, in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o F w/ hx CML s/p Allo transplant from MRD, hx of chronic 
GVHD, presented with acute exacerbation of abdominal pain and 
diarrhea, on levsin and rifaximin as this regimen has helped her 
in the past. 

#Abdominal pain and Diarrhea: Continued symptomatic improvement 
with Levsin and Rifaximin (she has responded well to this 
medication in the past) throughout admission. The patient had 
good PO intake while on rifaximin, tolerating meals well. She 
carries dx of gastritis and was previously treated for H.Pylori. 
Of note, extensive imaging performed in early ___ (CTA, RUQ 
ultrasound, MRI) revealed cysts of the pancreatic head. The 
current problem seems to be related to intestinal bacterial 
overgrowth. Contributing factors include: She  is on chronic 
PPI, omeprazole, which abates bacterial growth. Also,gut GVHD, 
causing a component of bowel neuropathy is also likely, and is 
complicated by hypogammaglobulinemia, as IgG levels have been on 
the low side, despite resolution of diarrhea. The patient 
received a full dose of IVIG on ___ after IgG value was 698, 
dose of IgG given in the hope that improving the 
hypogammaglobulinemia will improve the GVHD and improve sx's. 
Goal IgG level is between 700 and 1000, she will have outpatient 
followup and repletion if below goal. GI was also following 
throughout her admission, they believed her symptoms to be due 
to GVHD and small bowel bacterial overgrowth, and  recommended 
against any further imaging or treatment. They agreed with 
continuing rifaximin x2 week course and want her to f/u as 
outpt. She already has an appt ___. She will have an SIBO 
breath test done in the outpatient setting to definitively rule 
out the possibility of an H.pylori recurrence. Stool studies 
have been negative to date. For chronic pain, we are continuing 
MS ___ 15 mg BID; this is lower than her previous dose, but 
seems to be managing her pain quite well. On discharge, her 
abdominal pain was much improved and she had no diarrhea x72 
hours.

#Graft vs host disease- eye: pt has hx of loss of vision, 
presumably due to chronic GVHD. We arranged for her to get 
autologous eye drops for this.

#Nausea/Vomiting: Resolved. This could have been due to a 
transient viral episode or another manifestation of her chronic 
abdominal pain. Tolerating PO fluids. 
An abdominal xray was done which ruled out obstruction, we 
maintained adequate hydration with fluids as necessary and 
advanced her diet as tolerated. On discharge, she was tolerating 
meals well and had no nausea or vomiting.

#CML: Stable. Complicated by GVHD. s/p transplant in ___. She 
has continued her prophylactic medications.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o F w/ hx CML s/p Allo transplant from MRD, hx of chronic 
GVHD, presented with acute exacerbation of abdominal pain and 
diarrhea, on levsin and rifaximin as this regimen has helped her 
in the past. 

#Abdominal pain and Diarrhea: Continued symptomatic improvement 
with Levsin and Rifaximin (she has responded well to this 
medication in the past) throughout admission. The patient had 
good PO intake while on rifaximin, tolerating meals well. She 
carries dx of gastritis and was previously treated for H.Pylori. 
Of note, extensive imaging performed in early ___ (CTA, RUQ 
ultrasound, MRI) revealed cysts of the pancreatic head. The 
current problem seems to be related to intestinal bacterial 
overgrowth. Contributing factors include: She  is on chronic 
PPI, omeprazole, which abates bacterial growth. Also,gut GVHD, 
causing a component of bowel neuropathy is also likely, and is 
complicated by hypogammaglobulinemia, as IgG levels have been on 
the low side, despite resolution of diarrhea. The patient 
received a full dose of IVIG on ___ after IgG value was 698, 
dose of IgG given in the hope that improving the 
hypogammaglobulinemia will improve the GVHD and improve sx's. 
Goal IgG level is between 700 and 1000, she will have outpatient 
followup and repletion if below goal. GI was also following 
throughout her admission, they believed her symptoms to be due 
to GVHD and small bowel bacterial overgrowth, and  recommended 
against any further imaging or treatment. They agreed with 
continuing rifaximin x2 week course and want her to f/u as 
outpt. She already has an appt ___. She will have an SIBO 
breath test done in the outpatient setting to definitively rule 
out the possibility of an H.pylori recurrence. Stool studies 
have been negative to date. For chronic pain, we are continuing 
MS ___ 15 mg BID; this is lower than her previous dose, but 
seems to be managing her pain quite well. On discharge, her 
abdominal pain was much improved and she had no diarrhea x72 
hours.

#Graft vs host disease- eye: pt has hx of loss of vision, 
presumably due to chronic GVHD. We arranged for her to get 
autologous eye drops for this.

#Nausea/Vomiting: Resolved. This could have been due to a 
transient viral episode or another manifestation of her chronic 
abdominal pain. Tolerating PO fluids. 
An abdominal xray was done which ruled out obstruction, we 
maintained adequate hydration with fluids as necessary and 
advanced her diet as tolerated. On discharge, she was tolerating 
meals well and had no nausea or vomiting.

#CML: Stable. Complicated by GVHD. s/p transplant in ___. She 
has continued her prophylactic medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had this sharp stomach pain since yesterday, along with nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. It’s just like the last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it’s similar to your last episode. Was that treated with rifaximin and hyoscyamine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. That helped before, but it came back. The pain is worse this time, and I’m waking up at night from the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for that. We’ve started you on IV fluids and some pain medication. We’ll run some tests to make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also had a little cough and chills. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll check for infections, but it could be a mild viral thing. Your vitals are stable, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night are mostly normal. Your liver enzymes were a bit high, but not concerning. No signs of kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the diarrhea? I’m still having some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool. No C. diff, no salmonella, shigella, or other bacteria. So it’s not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we think it’s a flare of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth—SIBO. That’s what we treated last time, and it responded well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we’re doing the same treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting rifaximin and hyoscyamine. They stay in the gut and help reduce the bacteria and your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is a little better. I haven’t vomited since this morning. But I’m still bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now and advance your diet slowly. We also checked your CMV—came back negative, so that’s not contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that. What about my immune system? I know my IgG was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your IgG was 698 this morning—just below normal. We’re going to give you IVIG to boost it. It may help with both your gut symptoms and GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me feel better overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help your immunity and may reduce inflammation from GVHD. We’ll check your levels again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re doing well. Your pain is improving, and you kept down breakfast. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel like I can eat more now. Is the IVIG helping already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes time, but we’re on the right track. Your GI team agrees—this is likely SIBO and gut GVHD. No need for more scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they found a cyst on my pancreas. Should we check that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s stable and not causing symptoms. You’ll follow up with GI for a breath test to confirm SIBO and monitor the cyst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat stool tests are negative again. No parasites, no viruses isolated so far. Norovirus is still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. That supports our diagnosis of SIBO, not an acute infection. Your pain is much better, and you’ve had no diarrhea since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We’ll watch you for one more day to make sure you stay stable on oral meds and food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we arranged for autologous eye drops for your dry eyes from GVHD. You’ll get those soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My vision’s been blurry. I’m glad we’re addressing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night without symptoms. Great job. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I be on at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from rifaximin to Augmentin for one more week. It covers a broader range of gut bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the hyoscyamine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that three times a day. Also keep taking your omeprazole, prednisone, and other regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain medicine? I’m on MS Contin now twice a day instead of three times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. We lowered it because your pain is better. If it flares up, we can increase it. Use the immediate-release oxycodone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are stable. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but not new. We’ll check iron for your restless legs later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That tingling in my legs at night has been worse. I hope iron helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. We’ll discuss that with your hematologist at your follow-up in three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’ve had no pain, no diarrhea, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any diet changes I should follow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Limit dairy—lactose can worsen bloating. If you eat dairy, take Lactaid. For beans, use Beano to reduce gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI follow-up is scheduled. You’ll get the SIBO breath test there. And hematology for IgG check and possible IVIG if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to go. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic. Call if you have fever, severe pain, or diarrhea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. No pain, no issues. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: take Augmentin with food, keep using hyoscyamine, and follow the diet tips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with an acute exacerbation of chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea, consistent with her prior episodes. She was treated with rifaximin and hyoscyamine, with significant improvement in symptoms. Workup showed no infectious cause, supporting a diagnosis of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Hypogammaglobulinemia was confirmed with a low IgG level, and she received IVIG to support immune function. Her nausea and vomiting resolved, and she tolerated oral intake well. She was transitioned to Augmentin for continued treatment of bacterial overgrowth and discharged home with follow-up appointments in GI and hematology. Her chronic graft-versus-host disease was managed with ongoing prednisone and new autologous eye drops for ocular symptoms.
